one_liner: EA's from-scratch STL reimplementation for games; eastl::vector targets faster push_back/indexing than std::vector.
what_it_does: EASTL reimplements STL containers, iterators, and algorithms (vector, deque, list, hash_map, etc.) for game runtimes and tools, plus extras std doesn't have, like fixed_* (stack-allocated, no heap alloc) and intrusive_* containers. eastl::vector exposes the same template shape and most member functions as std::vector, so most call sites port with a namespace swap. The allocator interface, exception-handling toggle, and a few semantics (e.g. operator= doesn't copy the allocator) diverge from the standard, so it is not a byte-for-byte drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: EASTL avoids the deep, virtual-free but call-heavy chains that make debug-build STL slow, so its win is largest in unoptimized builds and on weak historical STL implementations (MSVC VC7/VC8, console STL). For trivially-copyable element types it uses memcpy/memmove during vector reallocation instead of invoking copy/move constructors per element (documented in doc/Gotchas.md). It also guarantees no allocation for a newly-constructed empty container and supports fully disabling exception handling, removing that overhead from the container/allocator path.
when_to_use: Game/console codebases where debug (unoptimized) container performance matters and you can standardize on one non-standard container library across all target platforms
Workloads dominated by push_back/reallocation of trivially-copyable structs, where the memcpy/memmove optimization applies
You also want fixed_vector/intrusive_list-style zero-allocation containers alongside vector, not just a faster vector
Targeting older or console toolchains (VC7/VC8-era, GCC 3.x+) where std STL implementations were measurably weak
You're comfortable vendoring a large source-drop plus its EABase dependency rather than a single header
when_not_to_use: You need a literal drop-in for std::vector with zero porting cost: allocator model, exception semantics, and operator= behavior differ

You're on an EASTL release older than 3.27.00 (Oct 2025): eastl::vector::push_back(v.back()) (self-referential push_back) silently corrupted data on reallocation (issue #524), fixed only in that release
Concurrent writers without your own locking: EASTL containers are not thread-safe for mutation from multiple threads, same as std::vector

You need certainty of a speedup on current hardware: the only public numbers are a first-party 2007 WG21 paper (evidence tier C) on Pentium 4/PowerPC-era hardware and compilers; libstdc++ push_back gain was only 1.02x and eastl::sort was 0.92x (slower) than std::sort on libstdc++
Sort-heavy workloads on libstdc++-class standard libraries, where the same paper showed EASTL losing to std::sort

integration.dependencies: EABase (EA's base config/type-traits header library; CMakeLists.txt fetches it via FetchContent)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 per CMakeLists.txt (target_compile_features cxx_std_14), but include/EASTL/vector.h currently uses unguarded `if constexpr`, which warns/fails below C++17 (open issue #587) -- C++17 recommended in practice
integration.platforms: any C++14+ compiler, 32-bit and 64-bit; no OS-specific code path required, historically used across PC, console, and Mac/Linux toolchains
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe for concurrent mutation of the same container instance; per doc/FAQ.md, EASTL uses no static/global state and leaves synchronization (e.g. a mutex) to the caller, same model as std::vector
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- explain: same template surface and most member functions as std::vector, but allocator interface, exception-handling toggle, and operator=() (doesn't copy the allocator) differ from the standard

gotchas: eastl::vector::push_back(v.back()) (self-referential push_back) silently corrupted data on reallocation before release 3.27.00 (Oct 2025) -- pin to >=3.27.00 (issue #524)
vector::operator=() does not copy the source container's allocator, unlike some std implementations
vector::size() is computed by pointer subtraction and can trigger an integer division when sizeof(T) isn't a power of two
Overriding the global allocator requires supplying EASTL's two custom operator new[] overloads, not a standard C++ allocator
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick eastl::vector when you want one consistent container ecosystem (fixed_*, intrusive_*, allocator model) across an entire codebase, especially on older/console toolchains, rather than swapping in a single faster vector type. For a narrowly-scoped, better-evidenced vector replacement alone, fast_vector or veque have more direct current benchmarks; plf::colony is the better pick if the workload is erase-heavy rather than push_back-heavy.
verified_claims_summary: The only available measurement is a first-party 2007 EA/WG21 committee paper (N2271, evidence tier C) comparing eastl::vector<uint64> against std::vector: push_back was 1.63x faster on Windows/Pentium4/VC8, 2.18x on a 64-bit PowerPC console/VC7, 1.02x on Linux/Pentium4/GCC4.1/libstdc++, and 1.59x on Mac G5 PowerPC/GCC4.0/libstdc++; operator[] on Linux/libstdc++ was 1.29x faster; sort on Linux/libstdc++ was 0.92x (slower than std::sort).
status_note: Actively maintained by EA (latest release 3.27.01, Nov 2025), BSD-3-Clause, 9,367 stars; usable via source-drop or CMake, but it's a large, non-trivial dependency (EABase plus a big header/source tree), not a lightweight vendor-in.
